Holy Roman Empire. A persistent misconception portrays the Holy Roman Empire as a continuous monolithic realm spanning medieval and early modern Europe. In reality, the HRE was a fragmented, decentralized confederation of hundreds of semi-autonomous territories nominally under the Pope's spiritual authority and the Emperor's loose secular overlordship, primarily centered in present-day Germany and Central Europe.

The Holy Roman Empire was not the Roman Empire revived. It began with Charlemagne's coronation in 800 CE and lasted until 1806, a break of over three hundred years from the Western Roman Empire's fall. The HRE consisted of hundreds of states, kingdoms, principalities, and ecclesiastical territories with varying degrees of autonomy. The Emperor had limited real power over them.

The title "Emperor" was conferred by the Pope, at least until secularization, and the position became hereditary in the Habsburg dynasty from the fifteenth century onward. Despite its name, the Holy Roman Empire was neither cohesive nor "holy" in any unified sense. It was a patchwork of competing interests bound nominally by the Emperor's authority. The Empire was primarily Germanic in character and scope, with its heartland in the German-speaking regions of Central Europe, not Italy or the Mediterranean.

The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 further weakened imperial authority by granting individual states near-sovereign control. The Empire dissolved formally in 1806 after Napoleon's victories.
